# 18-careforce — sources

Back-test entry `18-careforce.yaml`: Careforce, AI agents that call and book the patients a health center never reaches
(YC Fall 2024). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only, read that day. Quotes are verbatim from the page named.
"Author's choice" marks the smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent. The launch era is the
Launch YC post of 2024-11-22 and the weeks around it (the founder's gap-11 rule: every figure pinned to the launch era
where one exists; anything later is marked as later, and a later price sits under *Status today*).

Main sources (short names used below):
- [LYC] Launch YC: "Careforce - Must-have AI agents for Healthcare admin", 2024-11-22 (created_at in the page data) — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/MJj-careforce-must-have-ai-agents-for-healthcare-admin

- [CHCF] California Health Care Foundation investment page (CHCF is an investor, $500,000, February 2026; the page blocks direct fetches, so the quote is as the diversity research recorded it) — https://www.chcf.org/investment/careforce/

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Medical assistants at community health centers, who work the outreach lists between patients.
   [LYC] "For health centers & practices this means MAs (short-staffed with front desk and intake) end up spending most
   of their time on admin tasks and most patients are never outreached & scheduled for vital screenings/visits,
   leaving a 1/3rd of care unserviced." → `roles[assistant]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`. Author's choice: of
   [LYC]'s three segments (health centers and practices; digital health and CCM companies; payers) the first, the one
   the post describes by its staff.

2. **What (the job).** Get every patient due for a screening or visit called and booked.
   [LYC] "Most care coordination & data sharing is still manually done by staff through phones, email, fax because of
   unintegrated systems and custom workflows too unique to automate out of the box." → `statements.problem`,
   `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** Each working day, when the list of due patients has to be called between patients.
   [LYC] "Outreach using 50+ editable scripts (mammograms, pre-post-op, onboarding etc.)"; "Leave Voicemails, Sending
   reminders, and autonomously retry patients as needed". → `context.circumstance`, `occasion: outreach call list`.
   Author's choice: the window {5, WORKING_DAYS} (spec 120: a daily rhythm in a clinic read as working days) and
   Frequency 3 to 5 working days out of 5; [LYC] gives no count. Prevalence `p_80_100` follows from "most patients are
   never outreached".

4. **Which people.** US community health centers (FQHCs) and primary-care practices that work outreach lists by phone.
   [LYC] "Our AI agents are already Live with health centers and digital health companies helping analyze, call,
   schedule, and generate revenue." → `context.segment`, `market: US` (a San Francisco company, [KFF]).

5. **Who pays.** The health center. [LYC] "Let us take on your calling, coordination, and manual admin work so you can
   get more patients in the door without burning out your staff."; "increase revenue with Careforce AI Agents".
   → `persona.decision_maker: {role: director}`. Author's choice: the decider is the health center's executive or
   operations director and the tested role "The CFO" (a second role, "The board", listed: FQHCs are governed by
   boards). Purchase friction's three items (a HIPAA security review — tested; giving the agent access to the EMR; a
   board vote) are the author's, from [LYC]'s "Use EMR, Scheduling, payer and provider portals through UI or API
   Integrations" and [KFF]'s note that plans "are responsible for ensuring that technology complies with state and
   federal regulations, including patient privacy and data security". Commitment's step, "try it on one outreach list":
   [LYC] "We'd love to learn about your use cases and give you personalized demos unique to your use case."; the
   wording is the author's.

6. **Mechanism.** Two agents: one calls, texts, emails and books; one pulls data and builds the lists.
   [LYC] "Careforce creates autonomous agents that are able to take on these human-glue tasks and complete them in the
   same way as your staff would without the need for integrations." [LYC] (Angelica) "Call, text, email, and schedule
   patients autonomously"; "Speak in 29 Languages to engage and educate across demographics"; "Make 100 calls / min.
   and finish a year's worth of outreach in weeks". [LYC] (David) "Prepare reports, and generate lists for Angelica to
   realize the unrealized revenue". → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`; Compatibility (the list straight out
   of the EMR — tested; open slots; patients picking up unknown numbers) and Adoption friction (hand the day's list to
   an AI caller — tested; take the calls it hands back, from [KFF] "This will always be, in my opinion, an AI-human
   combination"). Relative advantage's two benefits are [LYC]'s retries (fewer_attempts) and "finish a year's worth
   of outreach in weeks" (shorter_time); the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** No price is public at launch or today: [LYC] offers demos, [WB] has no pricing page near launch,
   [SITE] has none today. The founder's price, AMOUNT_PERIOD **$1,500 to $3,000 per health center a month**, is the
   operator's reading: a monthly per-site fee of the size community health centers pay for a part-time outreach caller's
   share of work (an MA's hour is about $22, [BLS]; $1,500 to $3,000 is roughly 70 to 135 such hours), set below what
   the bookings it claims to recover would bring in. It is said in `statements.commercial` as the founder would type
   it, and marked there and in the header as the operator's.
   Existing sacrifice, RATE about **30% to 33%** of the patients due for a visit or screening per health center a month,
   lost as "Visits and screenings never booked because nobody reached the patient": [LYC]'s "1/3rd of care unserviced"
   for health centers (33%) and "costing 30% in bookings" across healthcare (30%). Ability to pay is read `budget` by
   the engine (a percent of patients never compares with an amount a month), so the directors answer the budget item.

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from [LYC]'s scripts list (mammograms, pre-post-op), the short-staffing it
   names, and [KFF]; no respondent is a real person. [KFF] (Kern's CEO) "But we are already stretched thin. We need this
   functionality to be much more effective and augment our efforts." [KFF] "In samples of actual conversations provided
   to a reporter, Angelica sounded lifelike at first, although more than once cross-talk with a patient caused the
   program to pause suddenly."

health center would pay. No respondent carries the name of a customer, patient, official or founder in the sources.

## Status today

Same idea, traction moved to health plans. [SITE] still sells the two agents for payors, plans, FQHCs and specialties.
The public customers are Medi-Cal health plans doing renewal outreach: [KFF] "Kern Family has spent about $370,000 on the
software by Careforce, a San Francisco startup, to facilitate rapid and repeated outreach to members when it's time to
renew their coverage."; "estimated it would have had to spend $2.4 million in staffing costs to match the program's more
than 800,000 calls to its 387,000 members"; "Kern Family's Medi-Cal renewal rate in April was 94.9%". [CHCF] "With the
aid of Careforce, KFHC renewed 96% of their members during the first year, compared to 38% before using the AI platform."
[KFF] says the agent "speaks more than 30 languages" (29 at launch). Price today: not public.

## Could not be sourced

- **A price, at any time.** The founder's $1,500 to $3,000 per health center a month is the operator's reading (item 7);
  the only public money figure is one health plan's cumulative spend ([KFF], 2026), not a unit price.
- **A health center's share of patients never booked, measured.** The 30% to 33% are the founders' own launch claims
  (one for health centers, one for healthcare overall), not a study.
- **A buyer title.** [LYC] asks "Healthcare Orgs" for demos; the director as decider, the CFO and the board as the roles,
  and the three Purchase friction items are the author's.
- **First-person MA accounts.** None public; the occasions are scripted from [LYC] and [KFF] (a health plan, not a
  health center).
- **A launch-era site.** [WB] holds no snapshot between 2024-05-18 and 2025-11-13; the launch post is the only
  launch-era page. [CHCF] could not be fetched directly (a bot check); its quote is as the diversity research read it.
- An MA's hour: [BLS]'s median stands in; no cost in the entry is in hours.

whys.g1: Both of us are saying the same thing — our system won't give the front staff the call list, so it comes to us on paper — and "The system can't produce a list" is exactly how I'd put it.
whys.g2: There's no junk answer on this line; both answers are about what got in the way.

founder.order_why: It runs the way I'd pitch Careforce: name and market, the MA's daily outreach list, the unbooked-patient problem, the calling agent and how it fits the EMR workflow, then who asks and who gets a link.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 5 carry the same kicker and question ('Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies.') on either side of the window screen 4, so it reads as the context being asked for twice.
founder.missing: The commercial side: nothing asks who pays or what they'd pay. My buyer is the health center's director (with a CFO and board), not the medical assistant, and my price is $1,500 to $3,000 per health center a month against 30–33% of due patients never booked. Neither the decider, the price, the cost it recovers, nor purchase friction (HIPAA security review, EMR access, a board vote) is asked, and screen 20 only sets up medical assistants as respondents, with no way to reach directors.

PRIMARY.order_why: It went from my own last few days, to the idea, to my last list, with the follow-up right after I said no, so each step led into the next.
PRIMARY.missing: After I said I didn't get everyone called and booked, nobody asked what stopped me: being pulled to room patients and cover front desk and intake, patients not picking up or needing a call in their own language, or getting them to actually book once I reached them.

screens.why1: Right after I listed what has to be true for Angelica to fit an MA's day, picking the one condition most likely to stop them is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: EMR, open slots and unknown-number calls are everyday words at a community health center, and the intro says plainly what to do.
screens.why3: These are my three conditions, and I know from our live health centers which one breaks first: lists built by hand from unintegrated systems.
screens.why4: The three are my conditions as typed, distinct from each other, and none is missing or odd for this pick.
screens.why5: The belief and test read 'the list came straight out of the EMR' word for word as I typed it, and nothing of Careforce or Angelica leaks into what a stranger is asked.

screens.why1: After saying how it fits the way MAs work today, asking what it does better is the obvious next step before checking what Keel wrote.
screens.why2: 'What does it do better than the way they do it today?' is plain to me, and the 25-word hint tells me how much to write.
screens.why3: I built Angelica around retries and finishing outreach fast, so the benefits are mine to name: no chasing patients through callbacks, and the whole list worked in one day.
screens.why4: It's a free-text box with one escape chip, and 'Leave this out of the study' is the right way out for a founder who doesn't want this tested.
screens.why5: I typed two benefits, but Keel's belief keeps only 'patients reached without calling back again and again' and drops 'the whole list called the same day', which is my 100-calls-a-minute claim.
screens.instead: Keep both benefits in the belief: 'For most, their last outreach list would have gone better with it: patients reached without calling back again and again, and the whole list called the same day.'

screens.why1: Right after I said what it does better than the way MAs work the list today, Keel shows the benefits it drafted from my answer, so this is clearly where to check them.
screens.why2: 'Outreach list', 'calling back' and 'called the same day' are how my MAs talk about the work, and both rows read on the first pass.
screens.why3: An MA knows whether her last list needed call after call to the same patients and whether she got through it that day, so both rows are things she lives.
screens.why4: The two rows are distinct, but the benefit I lead with is missing: more patients actually booked into visits and screenings ('book 30% more appointments'). An MA whose list went better would tick that first.
screens.why5: Mine retries for them, so the patient still gets called again and again, just not by the MA; 'reached without calling back again and again' drifts toward fewer calls. Keel also tests only that first row, even though the screen says all rows are equal.
screens.instead: What would have gone better on your last outreach list with it? — More patients booked into their visit or screening / The whole list called the same day / No more calling the same patients back yourself / Patients spoken to in their own language

screens.why1: After asking how it fits and what it does better, asking what my MAs must do to start is the obvious next step before the solution section closes (4 of 4).
screens.why2: "Setup, extra steps or learning" and the 25-word cap are plain, and I answered it at once in our own words: hand over the day's list, take the calls it hands back.
screens.why3: I know exactly what my MAs would have to change in their day, because the hand-off of the outreach list and the callbacks are what we design around.
screens.why4: The only option is the escape chip, and "Leave this out of the study" fits a founder who has no adoption step to test.
screens.why5: The belief keeps my tested step word for word (hand the day's list to an AI caller), and the second step stays listed rather than being merged into it.

screens.why1: Right after I said what they'll have to do to start using it, this is Keel's draft of those steps for me to check, so it's obviously in place.
screens.why2: Both lines are in a medical assistant's words (the day's list, an AI caller, take the calls), though the intro repeats the title word for word.
screens.why3: An MA who works the outreach list knows whether they would hand it over and whether they would pick up the patients who need a person.
screens.why4: The two steps are distinct and are the ones I meant, but the same thing is called 'an AI caller' in one row and 'the agent' in the next, which reads like two different tools.
screens.why5: The handover is kept as I typed it, but 'the calls the agent cannot finish' drifts a little from 'the calls it hands back'; my point was a deliberate handoff to a person, not a failure.
screens.instead: Rows: 'Hand the day's list to an AI caller' / 'Take the calls the AI caller hands back'

screens.why1: Right after I named the two efforts, picking the one most likely to stop medical assistants is the natural next step before Keel sets the test.
screens.why2: Hand the day's list to an AI caller and take the calls the agent cannot finish are how I'd say it to a clinic, and the intro is short and clear.
screens.why3: As the founder I know from demos that handing over the outreach list is the real hurdle for MAs, so I can pick from what I actually see.
screens.why4: Both options are mine and distinct, but one says AI caller and the other says the agent for the same thing, which reads a little uneven.
screens.why5: The belief and the test keep my words exactly, handing the day's list to an AI caller, with a sensible one-in-three bar.
screens.instead: Which one is most likely to stop them? - Hand the day's list to an AI caller / - Take the calls the AI caller cannot finish

screens.why1: Right before the study goes out is the obvious point to decide whether to turn yes-sayers into leads, and at launch I'm already asking healthcare orgs for demos, so a pilot ask is exactly what I'd want.
screens.why2: 'Pilot' is everyday language for me selling into health centers, and the hint shows the exact line respondents will see and where I'll find the yeses.
screens.why3: Whether I want follow-up conversations is my own call, and I can answer it instantly.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers it cleanly, with no overlap and nothing missing.
screens.why5: The screen keeps my 'Yes', and the respondent line says only 'try this for real' without leaking Careforce's name, Angelica, or my roles.
screens.instead: Keep it, but since my respondents are MAs who don't sign contracts, I'd word their line as "Would you want to try this at your health center? Leave your email."

screens.why1: Picking who will put my questions to the medical assistants belongs right before the link goes out, after the pilot offer and before sending.
screens.why2: The question is plain, but the hint says the interviewer is 'on video' while it only talks about recording a voice, so I can't tell whether my MAs will see a face; '400 credits, whichever you choose' also needs a second read to see it costs the same either way.
screens.why3: I know my MAs take these between patients at a busy health center, so I can judge which voice they would sit through after hearing a 5-second sample.
screens.why4: Two names with a play button cover the choice, but the names alone tell me nothing about how the voices differ (pace, warmth, accent), so I have to play both to choose at all.
screens.why5: It still says 'medical assistants', my respondents, and nothing about Careforce, Angelica or the health center buyer leaks into the interviewer screen.
screens.instead: Who should ask medical assistants your questions? (Same voice and cost either way; people can always read and tap.) — Daphne: calm, unhurried ▶ 5 s · Saskia: brisk, friendly ▶ 5 s

screens.why1: Right after choosing who asks the medical assistants, choosing how they answer is the obvious next step before sending.
screens.why2: Mostly plain, but the Daphne option is crowded: the repeated name, 'Hear her', the accuracy claim in a quiet versus loud room, and the status line all run together, so it takes a second read.
screens.why3: I know my MAs answer between patients, often in a noisy clinic and sometimes on a phone, so I can pick from what I know of their day.
screens.why4: Voice, text or let them pick covers every choice, the three options are distinct, and each readiness note (recording, ready now, ready when Daphne is) fits.
screens.why5: It keeps my audience as 'medical assistants' and nothing about Careforce or the agents leaks into the format choice.
screens.instead: How should medical assistants answer? — Talk to Daphne, an AI interviewer who asks aloud and shows each question on screen (works in a loud clinic, ready in a few minutes) / Read and tap, typing or speaking into any box (ready now) / Let each one choose when they open the link

screens.why1: Right after choosing how medical assistants will answer, I need to say how the links reach them; it is the last step before anything goes out, so it belongs here.
screens.why2: Two things need a second read: 'the Contacts page' names a Keel page I have not been shown anywhere in this flow, and each option's label runs straight into its description with no break ('People I know by name I send each one...')
screens.why3: I know whether I have named MAs at the health centers we are live with, or whether I would post in an FQHC or MA group, so I can answer this from what I actually do.
screens.why4: The three routes are named people, a Keel-found list and one open link in a group; they are distinct, cover how I would actually reach MAs, and 'People I know by name' fits the health-center staff we already work with.
screens.why5: Nothing of Careforce, Angelica or the director's role leaks into how the link is sent, and my pick, named people, is kept as I made it.
screens.instead: Who gets a link to the medical-assistant questions? — People I know by name: I send each one their own link / A list Keel finds for me (from Contacts): Keel makes a link per person, I send them / One open link I post where MAs already gather: each person signs in with Google first

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' is stated with '4 answered · 5 needed to call it' on each card, but the line under the title singles out Compatibility for no reason I can see, and the kicker's '7 people answered' sits beside '4 answered' without saying where the other three went.
screens.why_b2: There is no chart on the stage page, but each card's '4 answered · 5 needed' tells me what was counted, over how many and where the bar is; still, '3 too few' in the tally reads like a count of people when it means three cards, so I have to look twice.
screens.why_b3: The three dimension names and belief lines are exactly the ones I checked, but Keel's statement under the title is garbled ('the medical assistant one AI agent calls...', 'gets back patients booked... and lists of patients due for care'), so my own solution reads back mangled.
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what to do next, such as send the study to more medical assistants or how many more answers each card needs, or why only 4 of 7 counted; the 'What it measures' line explains the verdict rule, not my next step.
screens.why_b5: The page claims nothing beyond the data: every card says too few to call, and the n of 4 against a bar of 5 stays visible on each.
screens.instead: Too few to call on all three: of the 7 medical assistants who answered, only 4 were counted on each belief (3 had not worked an outreach list in the last 5 working days or could not say), and 5 are needed, so send the study to more MAs who work outreach lists by phone, and fix the solution sentence so it reads as I wrote it.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits beside its deciding number, 4 counted of 5 needed, and nothing else on the screen contradicts it.
screens.why_b2: The bars are plain, but the bar reads '3 of 4' over 4 counted while the verdict asks for 5, and the strip draws 5 cells with a ghost, so I need a second look to see where the line sits.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility and 'For most medical assistants, the list came straight out of the EMR' are exactly the belief I checked.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is wrong: 2 of 4 already said no, so even if Darnell counted as a yes, 2 of 5 is more than 1 in 3 and my belief cannot hold; the screen should say my EMR-pull assumption is in trouble.
screens.why_b5: The low n is said honestly, but the count line lists the yes answers and leaves out the 2 no's, and 'nothing is settled' hides that the bar is already out of reach.
screens.instead: Only 4 counted, but 2 of them build the list by hand or in a spreadsheet, so even a fifth yes would not reach your bar: plan for lists that don't come out of the EMR.

screens.why_b1: "Too few to call" sits right beside "4 answered · 5 needed to call it," so I know the status and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: I can see 3 better and 1 same out of 4, with Darnell as the ghost cell, but the bar written as "3 of 4" lands exactly on my own count of 3, so I had to look twice to tell my bar from my result and turn "no more than 1 in 3" into a count over 4.
screens.why_b3: The name Relative advantage and the line about patients reached without calling back again and again are exactly what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: "Nothing is settled here yet" is generic: it doesn't say the 3 of 4 lean my way or that one more counted MA would settle it.
screens.why_b5: n is visible, the small group is called a lean and not a call, Darnell's guess is left out, and nothing claims the belief held.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 3 of 4 MAs say it would have gone a lot better, which leans your way and would clear your bar; one more counted answer settles it. Olga, whose coordinator gets through the list, is the one it doesn't help.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' has its deciding number beside it, but the header calls it '4 answered' while the count line says 5 answered and 4 counted, so I have to work out that the shortfall is one more countable medical assistant.
screens.why_b2: The chart plainly counts yes or no on handing over the day's list across 4 people, with the bar at 3 of 4, but the one ghost cell on the strip needs a second look to tell whether it is Darnell's guess or the fifth person still needed.
screens.why_b3: Adoption friction and 'Most would hand the day's list to an AI caller' are the dimension and line I checked on the way in, word for word.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is the same generic line as the last two cards; it doesn't tell me to get one more medical assistant to answer, or that half my yeses depend on it being 'clearly worth it', which means the relative-advantage proof has to come first.
screens.why_b5: Even with 4 of 4 for me it claims no hold: it says the group is small, 'a lean, not a call', and keeps Darnell's guess out of the count.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 4 of the 5 who answered could be counted and 5 are needed; all 4 would hand over the list, but 2 only if it's clearly worth it, so get one more MA's answer and show them the bookings it recovers.

screens.why_b1: Each box opens on "Too few to call" with "4 answered · 5 needed to call it" right under it, so I know there is no verdict yet and exactly why.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility and Relative advantage carry my belief lines word for word as I checked them on the way in.
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what to do: not that one more answer would call these lines, not what two hand-built lists mean for an agent that assumes an EMR export, and Adoption friction is simply absent with no word on why.
screens.why_b5: The n is on every box, the low count is said plainly, and nothing claims more than two or one people said.
screens.why_b6: I did not type that the list is a manager's printed spreadsheet or a hand-filled clipboard, which says David has to build the list rather than pull it, nor that a practice with a coordinator is buried by prior auths and rooming instead.
screens.instead: Two of four had no EMR list at all (a printed spreadsheet, a clipboard), so lead with David building the list before Angelica calls it; one more answer would call these lines, and say why Adoption friction has no box.

screens.why1: A first question about whether I worked my call list belongs here, but this one asks whether I finished the whole list, and the next screen asks about my last outreach list, so the two don't match.
screens.why2: The words are mine, but 'called and booked' is two things, and I can call everyone without booking everyone, so I'd have to stop and decide which part you mean.
screens.why3: Working the due list by phone between rooming patients is my day, so I know exactly how far I got this week.
screens.why4: Almost no MA ever gets every single patient called and booked, so the honest answer, 'I worked the list but didn't get through it all', is missing, and that 'No' throws out the people who actually do this work; there are also two escape chips, and 'I can't recall one particular outreach list' doesn't answer a yes-or-no about the whole week.
screens.why5: Nothing leaks about a product, but the founder's goal of getting everyone called and booked has been turned into a pass-or-fail test of me instead of asking whether I had a list to call.
screens.why6: It's short and ends 'Yes or no', but 'called and booked' said in one breath is two questions, and a listener can't tell which one to answer.
screens.instead: In the last 5 working days, did you call patients from an outreach list of people due for a screening or visit? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after I said whether I got my whole due list called and booked, showing me a tool that does that calling is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: I know EMR, payer portals and no-answers, but 'the other' comes out of nowhere because it never said there were two AI agents, and 'integration project' is IT talk, not how I'd say it.
screens.why3: Calling, texting and booking patients off the outreach list between roomings is exactly what I do every day.
screens.why4: It's a card to read with no options.
screens.why5: The idea comes through, but 'the other' points to a second agent that was never introduced, and 'without an integration project' sounds like the builders' own pitch words rather than mine.
screens.why6: Said aloud, 'The other builds the lists' leaves me wondering which other, and the first sentence about one agent doing three things in 29 languages is a lot to hold in one breath.
screens.instead: Imagine Careforce, an AI that works your outreach list for you. One part builds the list from the EMR and insurance portals; the other calls, texts and emails each patient in 29 languages, keeps trying the no-answers, and books them in your schedule. The people building it believe it would talk to patients the way you would, without IT having to hook anything up.

screens.why1: Right after the idea of getting patients called and booked, it makes sense to ask where my call list comes from, since anything that does the calling would need that list.
screens.why2: Outreach list and EMR are words I use every day, so I can answer it on first hearing.
screens.why3: I work these lists between rooming patients, so I know whether I pulled mine from the EMR, got it as a report someone ran, or got it from the health plan.
screens.why4: 'Yes, with some steps' fights with 'straight out of', because if there were steps it wasn't straight out, and 'No' lumps together a payer gap list and a list I built by hand.
screens.why5: Careforce appears only on the idea card, which is shown on purpose, and the question just asks about my list, not their product.
screens.why6: It is short, asks one question, and has three options I can hold; I say 'E-M-R' out loud at work anyway.
screens.instead: Think of your last outreach list. Where did it come from? I pulled it from the EMR; someone ran it from the EMR for me; the health plan sent a gap list; or I put it together by hand. Or say you can't tell.

screens.why1: I just said my list didn't come straight out of the EMR, so asking what got in the way is the natural next thing.
screens.why2: EMR is plain to me, but "You said no to this: the list came straight out of the EMR" reads backwards and stiff, and I had to read it twice to see they meant my list didn't come from the EMR.
screens.why3: I know exactly why my list didn't come out of the EMR, whether it was the report missing people, me pulling it by hand, or the lead giving me a spreadsheet.
screens.why4: It's a box to type in, so there are no options.
screens.why5: It keeps the meaning, but "what got in the way" assumes the EMR was supposed to make the list, and at my clinic it may never have been set up to, so it drifts a little toward the founder's picture.
screens.why6: Heard aloud, the colon and the restated "no to this" clause sound awkward, and it takes a beat to hear it as "your list didn't come from the EMR" before the question comes.
screens.instead: You said your list didn't come straight out of the EMR. Where did it come from instead, and why?

screens.why1: Right after the card and the question about where my list came from, asking whether this thing would have helped my last list is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: "Go better for you" is loose. Better how: more patients reached, fewer calls, less time between rooming patients? I'd have to read it twice to decide what I'm judging.
screens.why3: I know my last list well, but the card only says "patients called and booked," so I'd be guessing what Careforce actually does before I could say if it would help.
screens.why4: A lot better, a little better, no difference, worse covers it cleanly, and "I can't tell" is the honest out given how thin the card is.
screens.why5: "Careforce, patients called and booked" is just the goal restated as a name, so it doesn't leak anything odd, but it also doesn't say what the thing is or does, which drifts from a real idea to judge.
screens.why6: Short, one question, four short options I can hold, and one escape said last. It says well.
screens.instead: Would Careforce have gotten more of your last outreach list called and booked, or not? A lot more · A few more · About the same · Fewer · I can't tell

screens.why1: After asking whether Careforce would have helped my last list, it makes sense to ask whether I'd actually hand my list over to it.
screens.why2: Handing over the day's patient list is how I'd say it myself, and I understand it on first hearing.
screens.why3: I work the list every day, but whether patient info can go to an outside tool is my supervisor's and compliance's call, so I'd partly be guessing.
screens.why4: 'Yes' and 'Yes, if it was clearly worth it' overlap, and there's no option for 'only if my clinic approved it', which is my real answer.
screens.why5: It stays on the idea card's own words, handing over the list so patients get called and booked, and nothing extra leaks.
screens.why6: It's short, one question, and four short options I can hold, with the escape said last.
screens.instead: To use Careforce, you'd hand the day's patient list to it. Would you do that, or not? Yes; yes, if my clinic approved it; probably not; no; or I can't tell.
